summary: Instructions from Bob Braden for connecting to IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) at UCLA's Campus Computing Network over the ARPANET. A user opens a standard Telnet connection to socket 1 and enters a TSO command. The note lists the possible replies, such as a welcome message or a notice that TSO is unavailable, and what to do next.

plainLanguage.summary: A how-to for dialing into a big computer at UCLA. You say a magic word, and it either welcomes you or tells you it is closed.

questions: how to use tso over the arpanet
subtitle: How to reach IBM TSO at UCLA-CCN over the ARPANET using a plain Telnet connection.

tldr.problem: Users on the ARPANET needed instructions for logging in to IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) at UCLA-CCN from a terminal on a remote host.
tldr.mechanism: The user makes a Telnet connection with ICP to Socket 1 at CCN, types the command TSO, and then converses line by line with TSO using a server Telnet that handles editing and character translation.
tldr.outcome: The note lists the possible responses, interrupt handling, line editing keys, timeouts and a workaround for a bug in the network interface to TSO.

today: RFC 377 has status Unknown and is not listed as updated or replaced. It is a usage note for one site's Telnet service in August 1972.

sections.title: Connecting to TSO
sections.content:
IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) is available at UCLA-CCN on Socket 1 using the standard Telnet protocol. The remote user performs ICP to Socket 1 at CCN and sends the command TSO followed by CR LF.

There are three possible responses. WELCOME TO UCLA/CCN TSO followed by a herald (!) means TSO is available, and a TSO LOGON command should follow. TSO NOT AVAILABLE AT THIS TIME means the user should check the TSO schedule or call the CCN on-line help phone. ALL TSO PORTS BUSY means to try again shortly, and to tell the Technical Liaison if this recurs often.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on the door with the word TSO. The computer says welcome, come back later, or all the seats are full.

sections.title: Talking to TSO
sections.content:
TSO is strictly line at a time. Input is not scanned until an end of line or an INS (interrupt) arrives, and TSO sends ! as a herald when it waits for input. Local echoing is required. The end of line indication is the standard CR LF.

A user can interrupt TSO output by sending an INS and DATA MARK pair (Telnet X'80'); TIP users can use the TIP command SEND SYNC. TSO treats this as an output break. The server Telnet disconnects the user if output to the network does not finish in 5 minutes, if an INS and DATA MARK pair does not match within 2 minutes, or if TSO waits 20 minutes for input.
sections.plainLanguage: You type one line at a time and press enter. If the computer talks too long, you can send a special signal to make it stop. If you wander off for too long, it hangs up.

sections.title: A Known Bug and Its Workaround
sections.content:
If a program has put the terminal in an input state and the user wants to suspend it without answering, an INS and DATA MARK pair is supposed to take control up a level. Because of a bug in the network interface to TSO, that interrupt is ignored in this case.

The workaround is to define a software break string, for example TERM INPUT (!!!!), with no quotes. After that, any input line containing four successive exclamation points is treated like an interrupt. If other characters precede them, the exclamation marks act as a line delete.
sections.plainLanguage: One stop button did not work in one situation. So the note gives a secret code word you can type instead.

sections.title: Character Sets and Line Editing
sections.content:
Both upper and lower case input are allowed, but the server Telnet translates lower case to upper, and output is normally upper case. Line editing is done by the server Telnet: CAN (control X) deletes the current line, BS (control H) deletes the previous character, and HT (control I) inserts one space. Other ASCII controls are deleted before editing.

Input is translated to EBCDIC by the rules used for a NETRJS remote operator console, described in RFC 189. For example, ASCII ! maps to a vertical bar and ~ to the EBCDIC not sign. Six ASCII graphics not in EBCDIC become question marks, and all Telnet controls except DATA MARK are ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The big computer speaks a different alphabet than your terminal. A translator changes your letters, makes everything capital, and lets you fix typos with special keys.

references.text: Braden, R. T., "Interim NETRJS Specifications", RFC 189, July 1971.
